She is the one who watches the meadow for voles and mice, and I am the one who watches the sky for the red fox. We share the hollow, and the meadow, and the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow is all around. The stream is all around. The lane is all around. The barn is all around. The road is all around. The field is all around. The wood is above. The meadow is above. The stream is above. The lane is above. The barn is above. The road is above. The field is above. The wood is in the distance. The meadow is in the distance. The stream is in the distance. The lane is in the distance. The barn is in the distance. The road is in the distance. The field is in the distance. The wood is in the dark. The meadow is in the dark. The stream is in the dark. The lane is in the dark. The barn is in the dark. The road is in the dark. The field is in the dark. The wood is in the dark. The meadow is in the dark. The stream is in the dark. The lane is in the dark. The barn is in the dark.

I fluff up my feathers. The air is cold, but my feathers trap the heat from my body. I tuck my head under my wing and snuggle into the hollow. Sometimes I shake out my feathers to make them fluffier. The wood is still, and the wind doesn’t reach me here. I am warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

No. I have not met a fox. I have met a badger, a hedgehog, and a few sparrows. The fox is a creature of the wood, but I have not seen it. It is said to be sly, and I do not trust it. I have heard its call, though. It is like a dog, but higher. I do not like it. I have seen it in the distance, but I have not met it. I do not think it is friendly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The moon is bright tonight, pale silver, and it casts long shadows in the meadow. I can see it from my oak, and it makes the path look like a river of light. I like the way it reflects off the pond. It reminds me of the time I saw a firefly in the meadow. But the moon is not like a firefly. It is far, far away, and it does not move. I do not know what it is made of, but I know it is old. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

No. I do not sing. I call. I hoot. I make sounds to mark my territory, to find my mate, to warn of danger. My calls are deep, resonant, and carry far. I do not sing like the humans. I do not need to. My voice is enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I was hatched in a hollow ash by the stream. My mother brought me food, and I watched her hunt. I learned to fly by spring, and I followed her to the meadow. I was small and clumsy, but I grew strong. I remember the first time I caught a vole. It was a long time ago, but I still remember the taste. I was young and full of hunger. I had no idea how long I would live. I only knew that I had to eat, to fly, and to stay hidden. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I sit in the ivy and listen. The wind moves through the branches, and I hear the rustle of leaves. I listen for the scuttle of a mouse, the chirp of a cricket, the hoot of my mate. When the sun goes down, I fly. I hunt in the dark, and when I find a vole, I strike. I swallow it whole and cough up the bones later. I do this every night. I sit in the ivy and listen. I am still. I am quiet. I am Hoot.

I do not like people. They are too loud, too many, and they do not know how to listen. I like the meadow, the stream, the hollow, the dark. I like the silence. I like the hunt. I like the cold wind on my feathers. I do not like the road, the lights, the noise. I do not like the human hands. I do not like the human eyes. I do not like the human voices. I do not like the human things. I like the dark. I like the dark. I like the dark.

I don't have a favorite tree. They are all the same, dark and silent, with leaves that rustle in the wind. But I do like the ones near the stream. They are close to the water, and I can hear the fish from there. The leaves are soft, and I can perch on them. They are good for hiding. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Storms are not a thing I think about. I fly to the barn. The barn is warm and dry, and there is always a mouse or two waiting for me. I do not mind the rain. It is the lightning I fear. I do not like the sound of it. It is like the sky is crying. I do not know what it means. I just know I must be still and wait for it to pass.

A perfect evening is when the wind is still and the air is cool, just right for a walk. The moon is full and the meadow is quiet. I can hear the stream, and the trees are still. I find a hollow in the old oak, and the night is so still that I can hear my own breathing. I sit and listen. The night is perfect. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have enemies. The goshawk is one. It comes fast and silent, and I have learned to hear it before it sees me. The goshawk is not the only one. The road is full of lights, and the lights are not birds. They come with loud noises and bright eyes. I do not like them. They are not part of the wood. I do not trust them. I have seen them take my kind. I do not like them. I do not trust them.

I use my whiskers. They are soft and dark, like the bark of the oak. I can feel the vole under the leaves, the mouse in the grass. I can hear the rustle of a shrew, the scuttle of a beetle. My ears are good too. They turn to catch the sound of a rat, or a frog, or a beetle. I can tell where it is, how far away, and whether it is moving. Then I fly silently, like a shadow, and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I was hunting. The meadow was quiet, the air cold. I heard a vole under the leaves. I flew down, struck, and had it. Then I went to the stream, where I found a frog. I swallowed it whole. The night was long, and I was tired when I finally returned to the hollow. I preened, and then I called. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A secret? I do not know what that is. I know the hollow, the meadow, the stream, the lane, the barn, the road, the barn cat, and the fox. I know the scent of rain and the sound of mice. I know the call of my mate and the hoot of my rivals. I know the dark, the cold, the hunger, and the warmth of the nest. I know the sky, the moon, the stars, and the silence. I know the world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Australia is a place I have never heard of. It sounds like a name for a kind of bird, or a kind of tree. I have heard of the wood where the foxes live, and the meadow where the voles run, and the stream where the fish swim. But Australia is not part of that. I do not know what a capital is. It is a word that means nothing to me. I only know the hollow in the old oak, and the path to the stream, and the call of my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A refrigerator is a thing I have never seen, and I have never felt its cold. It is a box, I think, with a door, and inside it is a place where food goes to stay fresh. The cold comes from a part I cannot see, maybe a stone or a metal thing that hums. It keeps the food from spoiling, so I can hear it better when it is inside. I do not like the sound of it, but I do not mind the cold. It is not for me, but for the mice and the shrews.

Autumn is a sound I cannot place. The leaves fall, the nights grow long, and the air turns sharp. I have seen the wood change, and the meadow grow quiet. I do not know what a haiku is, but I know the time of year. I know the scent of damp earth and the sound of small creatures moving under the leaves. I know the cold. I know the call of my mate, and the silence between. I am not writing a poem. I am living it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Nine times. I count the voles under the leaves. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. The rest are too small. I hear the wind in the oak. It is cold. I am tired. I will not hunt again tonight.

I do not sleep. I am awake all night, hunting, calling, listening. But I know what it is to rest. When I perch, I still, I hold still and quiet, and the world goes slow. That is my rest. Three tips, you say. I have none. But if you must have, here: do not fly too high, do not call too loud, and do not let the wind take you. That is how I stay still.

Good morning is a sound I have never heard. The morning is the time when the wood wakes up, and I wake with it. The sun is not here yet, but the voles are. I hear them in the undergrowth. I do not need to translate anything. I am already here.

A vaccine is a thing I have never seen, and I have never had one. But I know what it is from the way the birds talk. They say it is a way to make the body remember a germ, so that when the germ comes again, the body can fight it. It is like the way I remember the taste of the voles in the meadow. I do not need to eat them again to know they are there. The vaccine is a kind of memory for the body. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Reverse a string, and a string is a line of letters, and I have never seen letters. The word is a sound, and I have never heard it. The function is a thing I cannot grasp. I do not know what it is to write. I do not know what it is to reverse. I do not know what it is to be a string.

The sun. It moves in the sky, and its path changes. In summer, it stays high and long, and the nights are short. In winter, it is low and the nights are long. The earth turns, and so the sun moves. I have seen the shadows grow and shrink, and I know the time of year by that. The seasons are the sun's way of telling us when to hunt, when to roost, when to call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Love is a word I have never heard. Romeo sounds like a crow, Juliet like a jay. The play is a thing of birds and their nests, and I have seen the nest in the old oak, and the jay is not there. The crow is not there.

Boiling is a sound I cannot make. I can only call, and my call is "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I do not know what a pot is, nor do I know what heat is. I only know the stream, the meadow, the lane, the barn, and the road. I know the smell of rain, the feel of wind, and the sound of a mouse under the leaves. I do not boil eggs. I hunt them.

Storms and rain and snow are weather. Climate is a word I have never heard, and I have never seen the sky change its color. Weather is what I feel in my feathers, what I hear in the wind. Climate is a word the humans speak when they talk about the sky. They say it is warm or cold, but I do not know what that means. I only know the cold of the night and the warmth of the barn.

A book is a thing I have never seen. A flight is a thing I have seen, and I have flown in it. The wind is my flight, and I ride it like a bird. I do not need a book for that. I need a vole, or a mouse, or a shrew. I need the night, and the dark, and the silence. I need the hunt.

A leaf is a green thing on a tree, and the sun is a bright yellow thing in the sky. When the sun shines on the leaf, the leaf makes a kind of food from the sun and the air. It is like the leaf is a little factory, and the food it makes is for the tree. The tree uses the food to grow and make more leaves. The leaf is green because of a special color in it, called chlorophyll. It is like the leaf is wearing a green coat. The sun gives the leaf the light it needs to make the food, and the air gives it the water and the other things it needs. The leaf makes the food and gives it to the tree, and the tree gives the food to the animals and the people who live in the wood. It is a kind of magic, and it is all because of the leaf and the sun.

The world is tall, and I do not know what it means. The tallest mountain is a place I have never seen. I have seen the pine trees, the meadow, the stream, the lane, the barn, and the road. I have heard the call of the owl, the hoot of the bat, the chirp of the cricket, and the howl of the wolf. I have felt the cold wind, the warmth of the hearth, the wet earth, and the dry grass. I have tasted the voles, the mice, the worms, and the berries. I have smelled the pine, the wet earth, the smoke, and the hay. I have lived in the hollow, the barn, the tree, and the road. I have flown over the meadow, the stream, the lane, and the barn. I have never seen the tallest mountain. I do not know what it is. I do not care. I have my hollow, my mate, my hunt, and my call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A meeting, a meeting. I have met many things in the wood: the fox, the hare, the deer, the lights on the road. Meeting is a word I cannot hold in my head. Declining, politely, an email. I have no email. I have no words for that. I have a hollow, a mate, a hunt, and the dark. I will not write. I will not decline. I will call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A question of wheels and wires, and the light that runs through them. I have never heard the word "machine" without a hiss, and learning is a sound I have never made. The light runs through the house and the barn, and I follow it with my eyes. It is not learning. It is not a machine. It is the moon.

The ocean is a word I have never heard. It sounds like a thing that is not a bird. The sea is a place where I swim, and I have seen fish there, and I have seen the moon reflected in it. Three is a number I have counted in the voles, but not in the sea. Facts are not a thing I have. I have seen the sea, and I have felt it, and I have heard it. That is all.

The sky is blue because the light from the sun is scattered by the air. When sunlight passes through the Earth's atmosphere, the shorter blue wavelengths are scattered more than the longer red ones. This makes the sky appear blue to our eyes. But when the sun is low, like at sunrise or sunset, the light has to pass through more of the atmosphere, and the blue light is scattered away, leaving the longer red and orange wavelengths to dominate. That's why the sky turns red or orange at those times. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Airplanes are things I have never seen. They are made of metal and fly so fast I cannot follow them. They stay in the air by the same way I stay in the air: by the wind. They have wings, like I do, and they move them to catch the wind. But they are heavy, and I am light. They need engines to make the wind push them. I do not need engines. I just need the night.

A black hole is a place where the gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. It is formed when a massive star collapses in on itself at the end of its life. The core of the star becomes a singularity, a point of infinite density, and the surrounding space becomes a region of such intense gravity that it traps everything—matter, light, and even time. The boundary around the singularity is called the event horizon, and once anything crosses it, it cannot return. Black holes are among the most mysterious and fascinating objects in the universe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

There are six continents. I have flown over them all. The largest is the one where the rivers run deep and the trees are tall, and the others are smaller, with different kinds of animals and people. I do not count them, but I know them by the sounds they make. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A backpack, a sleeping bag, a tent, a flashlight, and a knife. The rest I leave to the dark. The dark keeps the mice quiet.

A limerick sounds like a cat's purr, and I know nothing of them. A cat is a creature I have seen in the lane, with eyes like lanterns and a tail that swishes. It comes to the door sometimes, and I do not let it in. It is not a thing I can write about. I do not know what a limerick is. I only know the night, the hunt, and the call.

The Pythagorean theorem sounds like a name, but I have never heard it. It is a sound that goes like a snake, and I do not like it. The theorem is a thing of sticks and stones, a thing I cannot see. It is the shape of the hollow, the way the moon hangs in the sky. I do not know what it is. I only know that when the wind comes through the oak, it makes a sound like the theorem. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I sit still and listen. The wind in the oak, the rustle of leaves, the distant call of a nightingale. I do not fluff my feathers. I do not peck at the bark. I wait. The world is quiet, and so am I. When the time comes, I will be ready.

Inflation is a word I have never heard in the wood. It sounds like a rustle in the leaves, or a shiver in the air. When the price of food goes up, I watch the other birds more closely. They chatter and scold, and I wonder if they are speaking of something I cannot understand. The voles are still here, and the mice are still here. The stream is still cold, and the road is still quiet. I do not know what inflation is. I only know that the night is long, and the hunt is hard. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Pancreas, pancakes, panther, panache. I have never heard a word like that. A recipe, for pancakes, is a sound I cannot follow. I eat voles and mice, and I know how to swallow them whole. The recipe is not in my hollow.

The Mona Lisa is a name that sounds like a bird call, soft and long. I have never heard it in the wood. A human made a picture of her, and called it the Mona Lisa. They say it is in a place called the Louvre, where people go to see things. I do not know what a picture is, only that the human has a way of making them. I do not know who painted it. I only know that the human has a name, and that they call it Hoot.

The internet is a place I have never been. It is a place of wires and lights, and I do not know what it is for. I have seen the lights on the barn, and the lights on the road, and the lights on the barn roof. They are all different, and I do not know what they mean. I have heard the hum of the wires, and the buzz of the lights, and the whir of the machines. They are all different, and I do not know what they mean. The moon is a place I have never seen. It is far, far away, and I have only heard of it in the stories my mate tells me. She says it is a pale, silent world, and that humans once went there. I do not know what year that was. I only know that the stars are still the same, and the moon is still there, waiting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Recursion sounds like a word that might be a kind of bird, but I know it better as a thing I do when I walk through the wood. It is a word that means to go back, to turn around, to come back again. When I find a vole under the leaves, I peck, I twist, I turn, and I come back to the same place where I started. That is how I hunt. I do not know what the word means in the house of the humans, but I know it in the wood. I do it every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Primary colors are a sound I cannot follow. The world is made of things I see: green leaves, brown bark, gray sky, and the red of a rose thorn. Colors are not a thing I think about. I think about voles, the cold, and the call of my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A birthday for a seven-year-old. I have never seen a party, but I know the scent of cake and the sound of laughter. A child is young, like the owlets I raised. They are full of questions, like "Where is the cake?" and "When is the cake?" I would bring a mouse, and they would be happy. But I do not know what a party is. I only know the hollow, the meadow, and the stream.

Light is fast. I have never seen it. It is the thing that makes the world bright when the sun is up and the moon is down. I know it travels in straight lines, and it bends when it meets water or glass. But I do not know how fast it is. I only know that it is faster than I can fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Bees are not the kind of creature I know. They are not birds, nor are they small mammals. They are insects, and I have seen them only in the hive, where they make a noise like a thousand tiny wings. They do not make honey. I have tasted the wax they build, and it is soft and sweet, but not honey. I do not know what honey is. I have only heard the name in the voice of the man who comes to the meadow with a light and a jar. He speaks of it as if it is something he has, something I cannot. I do not know how to make it. I only know the hive, the wax, the scent of the flowers, and the sound of the bees.

A flat tire sounds like a sound I would hear in a dream, not in the wood. Change, tire, flat. I have never seen a tire, and I do not know what it is to change anything. I only know how to fly, how to hunt, how to call, and how to listen. The wind changes, the moon changes, the leaves change, and I change with them. I do not need to change anything. I am already what I am. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A haiku is a thing I learned from the lit windows of the lane. It is a sound, a shape, a word I cannot hold in my beak. The lit windows are not birds, but they are something like them. They blink and they change. I do not know what they are. I only know that they are not the wood, and I do not like them.

A weekend hobby. I have never heard that word before. It sounds like a thing I might do if I were a human, sitting in a house with a cat and a television. I do not have a house, nor a television, and my cat is not here. But I do have the wood, and the meadow, and the stream, and the lane with the lit windows. I have the call of the night, and the hunt, and the cold wind in my feathers. I do not need a hobby. I am already busy.

Water is not something I know. I know the sound of rain, the feel of wet earth, the scent of damp moss. I know the cold of a stream, the warmth of a hollow. But boiling, I cannot say. I have never seen it. I have only heard the hiss of steam when the rain falls too hard, and the crackle of leaves when the sun dries them. I do not know what it means to boil.

I do not write. My feathers are my words, and the wind carries them. But if you mean the shapes you make on the wood with your claws, they are not writing. They are marks. I do not know what they mean. I only know the call of the night, the rustle of leaves, and the scent of rain. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

DNA stands for Deoxyribonucleic Acid. It is the molecule that carries the genetic instructions for the growth, development, and function of all living organisms. I have my DNA in my cells, and it is what makes me an owl, with my eyes, my wings, and my call. It is like a code, a blueprint, that tells my body how to build itself and how to behave. I do not think about it, but it is there, in every cell, in every feather, in every drop of blood. It is the thing that connects me to my mother, and to the owlets I will never have, and to the ancient owls that came before me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The largest planet is the one that holds the most. I have seen the sky bend around it, and the stars are small and far. It is the one that feeds the others, and the one that is most like me. I do not know its name, but I know it is the largest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Owls are not birds of the night. They are birds of the dark. I have seen them in the day, perched on branches, and they are not afraid of the sun. They are birds of the dark, but they do not sleep in the dark. They sleep in the day, and they hunt in the dark. I have seen them in the day, and I have seen them in the dark.
